notes.meaning: Korah was a Levite and a cousin of Moses and Aaron. He joined forces with leaders from the tribe of Reuben and 250 well-known tribal chiefs to rebel against Moses. They were jealous of the leadership roles God had assigned to Moses and Aaron.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this chapter as a combination of two older accounts, one about Reubenites resisting Moses' civil authority and another about Levites seeking the priesthood.

notes.meaning: The rebels gathered in a group and accused Moses and Aaron of setting themselves above everyone else. They claimed that because the whole nation was holy, no special leaders or high priest were needed. In reality, they were masking their own desire for power behind talk of equality.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching points to Korah's rebellion as a warning against rejecting church authority, arguing that the New Testament continues a distinct ministerial priesthood above the general priesthood of all believers.

notes.meaning: Moses immediately dropped facedown on the ground in humble prayer before the Lord. Instead of trying to defend himself with anger or force, he took the problem straight to God.

Moses told Korah and his followers that the Lord would settle the matter the next morning. God would openly show who truly belonged to Him and whom He had chosen to approach His altar. Waiting until morning gave the men time to reconsider and turn back from their sin.

Moses instructed Korah and his company to prepare censers, which were small metal pans used to burn sweet-smelling incense before God. Burning incense was the most sacred duty of the priests. Moses invited them to perform the very act they desired so God could judge them.

The men were told to put burning coals and incense in their pans before the Lord, and God would reveal who was truly holy. Moses turned their own words back on them, pointing out that it was the Levites who had crossed the line.

Moses urged the Levites who supported Korah to listen carefully to what he had to say. Because they were from his own tribe and already enjoyed a special sacred calling, their revolt was especially wrongful.

Moses reminded the Levites of the high honour God had already given them. The Lord had separated them from the rest of the nation to care for the tabernacle, God's sacred tent, and to minister to the people.
Even though God had brought the Levites close to serve Him, they were still dissatisfied. They let selfish ambition take over and demanded the high priesthood for themselves as well.

Moses pointed out that their rebellion was not really against Aaron, but against the Lord. Aaron was simply serving in the office God had assigned him, so grumbling against him was defying God's authority.
Moses sent messengers to summon Dathan and Abiram so he could reason with them. They stubbornly refused to come, showing complete disrespect for Moses and the authority God had given him.

Dathan and Abiram twisted the truth by describing Egypt, the land where they had been slaves, as a land flowing with milk and honey. They falsely accused Moses of trying to kill them in the desert and ruling over them like a tyrant.

The rebels complained that Moses had failed to give them fields and vineyards in the promised land, even though their own unbelief had kept Israel out. They asked sarcastically if Moses thought he could blind the people to his failures, repeating that they would not come.

Moses was deeply grieved and angered by their bitter lies and the dishonour they brought on God. He asked the Lord to reject their offering, pointing out that he had led them honestly and had never taken a single donkey or harmed anyone.

Moses repeated the challenge to Korah, telling him and all his supporters to present themselves before the Lord the next morning. Aaron would stand with them so God could openly decide who was His rightful priest.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think these verses repeat verses 6-7 and were added when the story was put together.

notes.meaning: Each of the 250 men was told to bring his own censer with incense before the Lord at the tabernacle entrance. Korah and Aaron would bring theirs as well, placing the whole dispute directly into God's hands.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view verses 16–17 as a later editorial repetition of the instructions in verses 6–7 that was inserted when the story took its final form.

notes.meaning: The next morning, each man brought his pan, placed burning coals from the altar in it, and added incense. They boldly gathered alongside Moses and Aaron right at the entrance to the sacred tent.

Korah gathered a large crowd of Israelites against Moses and Aaron, expecting the people to support his bid for leadership. Suddenly, the brilliant, awesome glory of the Lord appeared before the whole congregation, putting an end to Korah's boast.
The Lord spoke out of the bright cloud of His presence to Moses and Aaron. He was about to deliver His judgment on the rebellious gathering.
God commanded Moses and Aaron to step away from the crowd. Because the people had sided with the rebels, God warned that His wrath could consume them in an instant.

Moses and Aaron fell on their faces to plead for the very people who had opposed them. They appealed to God as the Creator who gives breath to every living person and knows every heart, asking Him not to destroy the whole community because of one man's sin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that the phrase 'God of the spirits of all flesh' is a later theological expression because similar wording appears primarily in later Jewish writings.

notes.meaning: The Lord answered the humble prayers of Moses and Aaron. In His mercy, He gave instructions that allowed the congregation a way to escape His judgment.
God told Moses to command the people to move far away from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. Staying near the rebels would mean sharing in their sin and their coming punishment.

Moses got up and walked straight to the tents of Dathan and Abiram, who had refused to come when called. The seventy elders of Israel followed him, showing united support for Moses and giving the moment solemn authority.
